title: Build a defensive local-security lab
summary: A consent-based home lab for isolating owned devices, inventorying listeners, observing network metadata, and running a contained decoy.

blocks.title: See your own network clearly
blocks.body: Build a small lab that makes exposed services, network zones, and decoy activity visible without testing anyone else's devices or traffic.

blocks.title: Consent is the first control
blocks.body: Use only equipment and traffic you own or are explicitly authorized to monitor. On a shared network, put the lab behind a router you control. Do not inspect a roommate's, guest's, employer's, or neighbor's traffic.

blocks.heading: A small, separated topology
blocks.alt: An upstream network connects to a lab router that separates trusted devices, a passive sensor, and an isolated honeypot with blocked outbound access.
blocks.caption: Repository-hosted diagram. The image widget can also use an approved HTTPS URL now, and a first-party object-storage URL later without changing the artifact shape.

blocks.heading: Give each part one job
rows: No inbound port forwards; current firmware; unique admin password
Copies authorized traffic to a sensor
Turns packets into connection and alert logs
Separate zone; no real credentials or data; outbound denied
blocks.caption: A repeater that only extends Wi-Fi may not create isolation. Use routing and firewall rules you can verify.

blocks.heading: Build in four reversible stages
items: Write the boundary: list the devices and traffic you are allowed to observe.
Place those devices behind a lab router or isolated guest network and verify that the lab cannot reach protected local networks.
Record listening services on each owned host, then close or document anything you do not need.
Add passive monitoring, and only then add one contained honeypot with outbound traffic blocked.

blocks.heading: Inventory listeners on machines you own
blocks.code:
# Linux
sudo ss -lntup

# macOS
sudo lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN

# Windows PowerShell
Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | Sort-Object LocalPort

blocks.heading: Treat the list as a baseline
blocks.body: For each listener, record the owning process, local address, port, why it exists, and whether another device can reach it. A service bound only to loopback is different from one exposed to every interface. Investigate unknowns before disabling them, and repeat the inventory after intentional changes.

columns.name: Zeek
columns.detail: Produces rich connection and protocol logs for understanding normal behavior and investigating events.

columns.name: Suricata
columns.detail: Produces alerts and structured EVE JSON records when rule-based detection is the main goal.

columns.name: OpenCanary
columns.detail: Runs lightweight decoy services and alerts when something touches them.

columns.name: Cowrie
columns.detail: Emulates SSH and Telnet for a focused decoy, with careful containment and log review.

items.label: Isolated from trusted devices
items.detail: Use a separate VLAN, interface, or downstream lab router.

items.label: Outbound access denied by default
items.detail: A compromised decoy must not become a launch point.

items.label: No real secrets or personal data
items.detail: Use synthetic banners, accounts, and files.

items.label: LAN-only first
items.detail: Learn the logs and failure modes before considering any internet exposure.

items.label: Retention and review defined
items.detail: Know what is logged, where it lives, and when it is deleted.

slides.title: Stage 1 · Know
slides.body: Inventory owned devices and listening services. Keep the first result as a dated baseline.

slides.title: Stage 2 · Separate
slides.body: Move experiments behind a boundary you control and verify firewall behavior from both sides.

slides.title: Stage 3 · Observe
slides.body: Add one sensor or decoy, confirm the logs you need, and keep retention deliberately small.

blocks.heading: Start with the boundary, not the honeypot
blocks.body: Draw your actual network, mark what you own, and inventory listeners on one machine. That evidence determines the next safe page in this series.
